report.source_text: An ophthalmic B-scan ultrasound showed retinal detachment with hemorrhage. Orbital MRI confirmed the thickening and strengthening of the right lateral wall, characteristics of metastatic carcinoma. The internal rectus and lateral rectus muscles were thickened and hardened, the 2-cm-long optic nerve was thickened, and its stump was invaded by the metastasis. The T1-weighted images of the MRI scans showed hyperintensity (Fig. 1), whereas the T2-weighted images showed hypointensity (Fig. 2). A contrast-enhanced MRI scan revealed inhomogeneous enhancement of the posterior wall (Fig. 3). The presence of lesions was associated with invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, and sclera by the metastatic cells.

report.source_text: Considering his severe eye pain and irreversible loss of vision, our patient had undergone right eyeball enucleation under general anesthesia on February 3, 2015. This type of procedure is indicated for patients who have had severe eye trauma and for those patients experiencing severe eye pain with unrecoverable vision. His complete eyeball was observed intraoperatively.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 43-year-old Asian man with a history of metastatic penile squamous cell carcinoma presented with right eye pain and vision loss. Initial ophthalmic B-scan ultrasound and orbital MRI revealed retinal detachment, hemorrhage, and findings consistent with metastatic carcinoma, including optic nerve, choroid, and sclera invasion. Due to severe eye pain and irreversible vision loss, the patient underwent right eyeball enucleation on February 3, 2015. Histopathological examination of the enucleated tissue confirmed metastatic moderately differentiated penile squamous cell carcinoma infiltrating various ocular structures. The patient subsequently received chemotherapy and radiotherapy and died 6 months later due to brain metastasis.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with right eye pain and vision loss, with a known history of metastatic penile squamous cell carcinoma.

Initial imaging (ophthalmic B-scan ultrasound and orbital MRI) showed retinal detachment with hemorrhage, thickening of the right lateral wall, thickened optic nerve with invasion, and invasion of choroid and sclera by metastatic cells.
Right eyeball enucleation was performed on February 3, 2015, due to severe eye pain and irreversible vision loss.

Histopathological examination of the enucleated tissue confirmed metastatic moderately differentiated penile squamous cell carcinoma infiltrating the sclera, choroid, retina, optic nerve, and external intraocular sites, showing keratin pearls, infiltrative growth of keratinized cells, and intercellular bridges.
The patient received chemotherapy and radiotherapy and died 6 months later due to brain metastasis.
